![](images/penguins.jpg)

*Data in the Wild* introduces students to data science through the R programming language, applied to real ecological and conservation challenges. The course is built around a narrative, a mission to establish a sustainable colony in Antarctica, in which each module presents a new crisis for students to investigate using data. No prior programming experience is required.

The course was developed by Drs. Katy Prudic, Jeff Oliver, Keaton Wilson, and Ellen Bledsoe with support from the NSF Harnessing the Data Revolution program, and is taught at the University of Arizona as part of the general education curriculum.

## **The Narrative**

### **Module 1: Mission Antarctica!**

The team has arrived in Antarctica and must set up the tools needed for all future data work. Students learn the basics of R and RStudio in Posit Cloud: navigating the interface, writing and running code, creating objects, working with vectors and data types, and importing datasets. They practice summarizing data frames and computing simple descriptive statistics. By the end of the module, students can use R to explore ecological data and are prepared for data visualization and deeper analysis in later modules.

### **Module 2: Good Food Gone Bad**

A wave of food poisoning spreads through the team, and the colony must identify the source. Students use descriptive statistics and data visualization to explore dietary and aquaculture data and investigate whether plants or fish are responsible. They create and interpret histograms, scatterplots, and multi-group comparisons using both base R and ggplot2, learning how visual cues reveal patterns in single variables and relationships between variables. By the end of the module, students can summarize numeric data, choose appropriate plot types, compare groups visually, and use evidence from distributions and densities to identify which fish species and environmental conditions are driving the sickness.

### **Module 3: Follow That Seal**

Leopard seal activity is disrupting fishing operations, and unreliable radio collars are making it difficult to track seal behavior safely. Students begin by cleaning multiple datasets on collar battery life and signal distance, then use t-tests and ANOVA to compare performance across manufacturers. They apply K-Nearest Neighbors to classify unlabeled collars and determine which supplier is producing faulty equipment. The module introduces regression: first simple linear regression to model relationships between ecological variables, and then multiple regression and interaction terms. By the end of the module, students can test group differences, fit and interpret linear and multiple regression models, and use a simple machine-learning method to support ecological decision-making.

### **Module 4: March of the Penguins**

To build a sustainable fishery, the team must understand how local Antarctic fish populations grow and respond to harvesting. Students begin by exploring exponential and logistic population growth, interpreting the intrinsic rate of increase and carrying capacity. They visualize population trajectories, compare species, and identify which populations are stable or declining. Students then fit logistic growth models using the `drc` package to estimate carrying capacity more accurately, and use those estimates to calculate the maximum sustainable yield. Then, they compare multiple fish populations by adding logistic model curves to their plots and testing differences statistically with ANOVA and post-hoc comparisons. By the end of the module, students can model population dynamics, estimate sustainable harvest levels, and use data-driven evidence to recommend which fish population is safest to fish.

## **Learning Objectives**

By the end of the course, students will be able to:

1. Work with ecological data in R, including importing, cleaning, summarizing, and organizing datasets.
2. Visualize patterns and relationships using appropriate plots.
3. Apply statistical methods including t-tests, ANOVA, and regression to evaluate ecological questions.
4. Fit and interpret ecological models, including logistic growth and carrying capacity, to support management decisions.
5. Communicate data-driven conclusions clearly.

## **For Instructors**

Course materials, including student and instructor versions of all lessons, datasets, and assignments, are openly available and designed to be adaptable for other institutions and programming languages. R is used throughout, but the course structure is transferable to Python or other environments.

All materials are available on the [course site](structure.qmd) and in the [GitHub repository](https://github.com/BiodiversityDataScienceCorp/DataInTheWild_UA).
